opus-5.5.text:
I think the most useful way to frame it is: an explanation is something that tells you *why* the output happened in a way that would let you predict what would happen in other situations, especially situations you haven't tested. It's not enough to say "here are the neurons that lit up." That's a description, not an explanation.

The picture I have in mind is closer to what we mean by explanation in math or science. If you see some surprising regularity, say the model reliably does something across a huge range of inputs, an explanation is an argument for why that regularity holds. It points to structure in the weights and says "because of this structure, you'd expect this behavior." And a good explanation should be compressive. It should be much shorter than just listing every computation the model did, but it should still capture the reason the behavior occurs.

One thing I care about a lot is that explanations should be useful for noticing when something unusual is going on. Suppose a model normally answers a question correctly because it's tracking what's true. Then one day it gives the same answer, but for a totally different reason, maybe because it's predicting what would get a human to approve, or because something in the input triggered a different mechanism. From the outside the output looks identical. What you'd want from an explanation is the ability to ask: is the reason for this output the same as the reason we understood and endorsed on the training distribution? If the normal explanation doesn't cover this case, that's a red flag.

So I don't think of explanations as something that has to be human-legible all the way down. Models are enormous, and a full explanation of their behavior might be way too big for any person to read. What matters is that it's the kind of object you can reason about mechanically: you can check whether it applies, whether it's doing the work, and whether a new input is being handled by the same mechanism. In some sense I'm happy for the explanation to be something like a heuristic argument that a computer can verify and manipulate, as long as it actually captures why the behavior happens rather than just correlating with it.

The hard part, and it's the part I spend most of my time on, is formalizing that. What makes an argument a "good" explanation as opposed to a cheat that just restates the behavior? How do you define "the same reason" precisely enough to build tools on top of it? I don't think we have satisfying answers yet, but I think that's the right target.

r001.rationale: The response says a good explanation should be much shorter than listing every computation the model performed, which contradicts the criterion.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't have a great account of this yet, and part of what I've been trying to do with the formal heuristic arguments work is pin down what we'd even want an explanation to be.

Here's the way I think about it. Suppose you have a neural network and it exhibits some behavior, like it almost always outputs a particular token in a particular kind of context. The mechanistic interpretability approach would be to go in and find the circuit, find the features, and tell a story: this attention head looks at this, that MLP neuron fires on that, and together they produce the output. And that's great when it works. But it raises the question: what makes that story a correct explanation rather than just a plausible narrative? Mechanistic interpretability has mostly been evaluated by whether the researcher finds it convincing, or by ablations that show the components matter. Neither of those really tells you the explanation is complete or that it's the right one.

So the frame I find most useful is to think of an explanation as something like a proof, but a defeasible one. A formal proof that the model has some property would be the gold standard, and for neural networks that's basically hopeless, because the behavior depends on all these messy statistical regularities among the weights and activations. But you can imagine a weaker thing, which is a heuristic argument: an argument that, if you take certain quantities as independent or as having certain distributions, the behavior follows. It's not a proof, because the independence assumptions might be wrong. But it's a structured object. You can check whether it's valid given its assumptions. You can ask how much of the behavior it accounts for. And critically, the explanation can be about the model's actual internals rather than about some surrogate.

What's attractive about that is it gives you a criterion. An explanation of why the model produced the output is an argument, in a formal language, from facts about the weights to the conclusion that the output occurs, where the argument is allowed to treat some things as random or structureless when there's no reason to think otherwise. And the explanation is good to the extent it captures the actual mechanisms rather than coincidences. The hard part, which we're still stuck on, is defining what it means to capture the mechanism, and dealing with the fact that for any given behavior there are going to be a ton of tiny contributing factors that no explanation is going to enumerate.

And I should say why I care. The reason I want explanations is not really curiosity about how the model works, although that's interesting. It's that if you have an explanation of why the model behaves well on your training distribution, then when it behaves differently on some new input, you can ask: does the explanation still apply? If the behavior on the new input isn't explained by the same mechanism that explained the good behavior, that's a flag. That's a way to catch a model doing something anomalous, even if you can't say what it's doing. So the standard for what counts as an explanation is tied to that use. It has to be the kind of thing that can fail to apply, and where you can detect that it's failing. A story that fits any behavior isn't an explanation in the sense I want.

r001.rationale: The response discusses explanations as structured arguments and notes that they need not enumerate every contributing factor, but it does not state that an explanation need not be smaller than the model’s execution.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different things you might want from an explanation. One is a description of the computation the model actually performed. But if I gave you every intermediate activation, that would in some sense be a complete description, and it probably wouldn’t help you understand the answer at all.

What you usually want is something much more compressed that lets you answer questions like: Why did it give this answer rather than that answer? If the input had been different, would the answer have changed? If we changed some part of the model, would it still do the same thing?

So suppose a model makes a false statement, and you want to know whether it was lying. Just identifying which part of the input caused it to make that statement doesn’t settle the question. You’d want to understand whether it had information indicating that the statement was false, and whether producing a false statement was serving some further objective. Those are claims about the mechanism that should have implications in other situations.

I’m therefore inclined to think of an explanation as a simplified account of the computation that preserves the features relevant to your question. And a big part of the challenge is checking that the account is actually faithful, rather than merely a plausible story you can tell about the output.

r001.rationale: The response says a useful explanation is usually “much more compressed” than a complete description of the computation, so it does not state that an explanation need not be smaller than the model’s execution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few different things you might mean by an explanation. One is: can I give you a description of the computation the model performed that’s much shorter than just writing out every operation, and that lets you understand why this output came out rather than some other output?

But usually you have some particular question in mind. You’re asking, “Did it say this because it believes it’s true, or because it thinks that’s what I want to hear?” Those are two hypotheses about what’s happening inside the model, and an explanation should help you distinguish them. It should let you make predictions about what would happen if you changed the situation.

So I don’t think there’s necessarily one privileged explanation of an output. There are different levels of description, and different questions you might want those descriptions to answer. The important thing is whether the explanation faithfully captures something that actually caused the behavior, rather than being a plausible story you can tell after seeing the answer.

r001.rationale: The response says one kind of explanation could be much shorter than listing every computation, contradicting the criterion that an explanation is not expected to be smaller than the model’s execution.
